awd_titl_txt: SBIR Phase I: Separation of Clean Gypsum from Phosphate Ore Processing Waste
awd_abstract_narration:
The broader/commercial impact of this Small Business Innovation Research (SBIR) Phase I project is in safe and economic isolation and disposal of radioactive components of phosphogypsum (PG), a problematic waste byproduct of fertilizer production, and converting the remainder waste into economically viable chemicals such as calcium carbonate & ammonium sulfate while recovering rare earth elements (REE).  Currently, over 70 million tons of PG are produced each year, with over 1 billion tons stored in Florida alone. Improper storage risks contaminating groundwater and harming nearby communities by allowing radioactive elements and heavy metals to leach into aquifers. Moreover, radium in PG can decay into radon, a carcinogenic gas. The proposed innovation aims to address those environmental risks directly and offers substantial commercial opportunity by generating up to $50 million in annual revenue per processing facility, cleaning and converting over 200,000 tons of PG per year. Thus, this innovation addresses a pressing need for sustainable waste management, mitigates groundwater contamination risks, and transforms problematic waste into economically viable resource.


PG is a byproduct of phosphoric acid production and includes naturally occurring radionuclides, making the material radioactive. These radionuclides are found in phosphate rock and are mostly uranium, thorium, and radium. This project focuses on developing an innovative, eco-friendly process technology that employs double salt formation using one or more ionic salt solutions to release all the contaminants from the gypsum crystal structure. After separating the double salt from those contaminants, gypsum is regenerated and converted into ammonium sulfate and calcium carbonate through the company’s proprietary process that uses flue gas as a source of CO2.  The contaminants can be either separated or disposed of safely. The project aims develop process conditions that achieve consistently high separation efficiency for broad range of PG feedstocks.

This award reflects NSF's statutory mission and has been deemed worthy of support through evaluation using the Foundation's intellectual merit and broader impacts review criteria.

Spearstone Solutions NSF SBIR Phase 1 Award #2437985 - Project Summary
Project Title: Separation of Clean Gypsum from Phosphate Ore Processing Waste

Phosphogypsum (PG) is a large-volume industrial byproduct generated during the production of phosphoric acid, a key input for fertilizer production. The phosphate ore is mixed with sulfuric acid to generate phosphoric acid. The resulting phosphogypsum contains trace impurities, including heavy metals and radionuclides like uranium, thorium, and radium. The Environmental Protection Agency (EPA) limits PG’s reuse and maintains that it much be stored in areas called stacks to limit exposure to radon gas, a result of radium decay. In the United States alone, millions of tons of PG are produced each year, and even more is stored in stacks where it poses long-term environmental, land-use, and regulatory challenges.

As stockpiles grow, there is a need for safe, scalable, and economically viable pathways to convert PG into useful products. While some technologies have explored chemical conversion routes, many face challenges related to impurity removal, product quality, or economic feasibility. In particular, the presence of radionuclides and trace contaminants can prevent the resulting materials from meeting the quality standards required for broader industrial markets. Without effective purification, these approaches struggle to deliver both environmental benefit and commercial viability. The NSF SBIR project proposes a novel approach to cleaning PG to remove the impurities and radionuclides, allowing it to be converted to beneficial products. Particularly, Ammonium Sulfate and Calcium Carbonate, an industrial mineral used in applications ranging from plastics to paper, and coatings. Additionally, the project explores the extraction of rare earth elements and high valuable metals from the PG.

The NSF SBIR Phase I project aimed to demonstrate the feasibility of Spearstone Solutions’ process for addressing the challenges related to PG and converting it into a product available for further beneficiation instead of long-term storage. The study employed a phased approach with the activities focused on developing proper protocols for handling and disposal of the extraction waste, demonstrating impurity and radionuclide removal from PG, with quantification of REEs, optimization of process parameters, and achieving complete bench-scale conversion of the cleaned PG. The objectives and outcomes are defined below:

  1. 1.     Establish Safe Handling & Regulatory Compliant Protocols. This effort established safe, documented laboratory practices for handling PG and clarified the key federal regulatory requirements relevant to future scale-up. The work resulted in a compliance roadmap to guide the design and operation of future facilities along with organization readiness to handle a scale-up when dealing with radionuclides. 
  2. 2.     Conduct Bench-Scale Extraction & Rare Earth Element (REE) Recovery. Testing confirmed that impurities and radionuclides can be separated from phosphogypsum, enabling purification of the gypsum material. The study also demonstrated recovery of rare earth elements while defining operating conditions that are effective across different PG sources.  
  3. Demonstrate Conversion to Value-Added Products. Cleaned PG was successfully converted to bench scale into high-value products using a patented reaction process. The work achieved high conversion efficiency and verified that the resulting calcium carbonate meets key quality metrics, including brightness and whiteness.

 

The Phase I project successfully demonstrated the technical feasibility of Spearstone Solutions’ process. Success was measured based on the following:

  • ≥90% of impurities, trace elements, and REEs within the PG sample removed.
  • ≥90% of PG converted to Calcium Carbonate
  • Quality and purity of calcium carbonate produced.
  • Calcium Carbonate: ≥90% pure, TAPPI/ISO brightness of >90 and CieLAB L whiteness > 90. High quality target being 95.

 

Bench-scale testing confirmed that PG can be treated to remove radionuclides, impurities, and recoverable REEs under a range of controlled conditions. The cleaned material was then reliably converted to calcium carbonate with high purity and yield, confirming that the chemistry and separation steps are reproducible and scalable.

These outcomes provide strong evidence that the process is not only scientifically valid but also technically viable for scale-up. No critical barriers were identified that would prevent further development, though optimization of operating parameters and continuous process integration remain the focus. The demonstrated feasibility mitigates the risks for future efforts and lays the foundation for eventual commercial adoption.

The broader impacts of this technology are significant. Environmentally, converting PG into useful products can reduce the need for long-term storage and lower the risk of stack failures. Economically, the rare earth elements and high-value metals and the ability to produce high-quality calcium carbonate from an existing waste stream creates opportunities for domestic manufacturing, job creation, and more resilient supply chains for critical industrial materials. Societally, improved PG management supports safer communities and more sustainable fertilizer production practices.

By focusing on material purity, product quality, and practical performance metrics, this project aligns with national priorities in sustainable resource use and circular economic development, while delivering tangible public benefits through environmental protection and economic growth.
